title: Verb Classes
short: Verbs fall into classes: strong roots (sḏm), third-weak (mrj "love", jrj "do"), doubled (mꜣꜣ "see"), and causatives in s- (sꜥnḫ "make live").
trouble: Students read the final weak consonant of mrj in every form. Third-weak verbs often lose it in writing.

blocks.html: Every verb has a root (Verb Roots). Grammars sort verbs into classes by the shape of that root, because the shape decides how the verb behaves in its forms.

The main classes: strong verbs, whose consonants all stay put (sḏm "hear"); third-weak verbs, ending in a weak j that usually drops (mrj "love", jrj "do"); second-geminate verbs, whose last two consonants are the same (mꜣꜣ "see"); causatives in s- (sꜥnḫ "make live"); and a handful of irregular verbs.

The weak consonants j and w were close to vowels. When a vowel or an ending stood next to them, they could vanish in speech, so the scribes stopped writing them. A doubled consonant behaves in a similar way: in some forms both consonants were heard and written, in others they merged into one. Strong consonants never disappear, so strong verbs look the same in every form.

blocks.cap: Gardiner names the weak classes with Latin abbreviations: 3ae inf. (tertiae infirmae) and 2ae gem. (secundae geminatae).

blocks.cap: jr.n=f "he did": the eye writes jr; the root jrj has lost its weak j.

blocks.title: Which class?
blocks.q: Is gmj "find" strong, third-weak or second-geminate?
steps: Look at the end of the root: g, m, then j.
A final j is a weak consonant.
So gmj is third-weak: "he found" is gm.n=f, with no j.

blocks.title: A doubled verb
blocks.q: Why does mꜣꜣ "see" count as second-geminate?
steps: Its second and third consonants are the same: ꜣ and ꜣ.
Verbs like that sometimes write the doubled consonant and sometimes only one: mꜣꜣ=f and mꜣ=f are both forms of "see".
blocks.a: Its last two consonants are the same.

blocks.html: Reading the weak j in every form. Students who learn mrj "love" go looking for a j in mr.n=f. Third-weak verbs often lose the j in writing, so the stem is just mr. Check: if a verb seems to have only two consonants and it is not in your list of two-consonant verbs, try adding a final j before you look it up.
Learn the class with the meaning when you learn a new verb, the way you learn a noun's gender. The next lessons on causatives and irregular verbs look at the last two groups more closely.
